passage:
In Class 9 I decided I needed to be on the quiz team, and Lokesh Sir picked the team. So I started telling him things. "Sir, your explanations are so much better than last year's." "Sir, that tie really suits you." "Sir, everyone says you're the best." I stayed behind to carry his books.
I wasn't actually thinking about his teaching. I was thinking about the list on the notice board.
One day he said, kindly, "Ayesha, thank you. The selection is a written test, though." My face went hot. He had seen through it, and he wasn't even angry.
Looking back, what embarrasses me isn't that I wanted the team. It's that I never once looked at him as a person, only as a door I wanted open.

qa.q: How did Lokesh Sir say the team would be selected?
qa.a: He said the selection is a written test.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when Lokesh Sir mentioned the written test?
qa.a: Ayesha felt embarrassed, face going hot, realising Lokesh Sir had seen that the praise was aimed at the team place, not at him.

qa.q: What could Ayesha have done instead to try for the quiz team?
qa.a: Ayesha could have prepared for the written test and asked Lokesh Sir honestly how to get ready.

qa.q: How might Lokesh Sir have seen Ayesha's compliments?
qa.a: He seemed to see they were aimed at the selection, but he responded kindly rather than angrily.

grounding: A teenager looks back on showering a teacher with compliments to win a team place, praise aimed at an outcome rather than the person.

passage:
Coach's note, Under-16 football, 12 October.
For three weeks Asif has been following our captain, a Class 12 student, everywhere. He carries the captain's kit bag, laughs at every joke, and tells anyone nearby that the captain is "the best player this school has ever had". The captain told me, a little uncomfortably, that Asif keeps asking if he'll "put in a word" for the starting eleven.
Asif's own training has dropped off. He skipped two fitness sessions to watch senior practice instead.
Today I spoke to him privately. I said I've noticed the compliments, and that selection depends on what I see on the pitch, not on who the captain likes. He looked embarrassed. We agreed he will do extra passing drills on Tuesdays, and I'll give him honest feedback every Friday.
Nirmala Joseph

qa.q: How many fitness sessions did Asif skip?
qa.a: He skipped two fitness sessions to watch senior practice.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when the coach mentioned the compliments?
qa.a: Asif looked embarrassed, since he had hoped the praise would get the captain to put in a word for the starting eleven.

qa.q: What did the coach do that could redirect Asif?
qa.a: The coach spoke to him privately, explained that selection depends on the pitch, and set extra passing drills with honest Friday feedback.

qa.q: How does the captain feel about Asif's praise?
qa.a: The captain seems uncomfortable, sensing the compliments are tied to a favour rather than real admiration.

grounding: A coach notices a teenage boy flattering an older student to win a team place, praise aimed at the outcome rather than the person.

passage:
Monday night
Today I told Ritu Ma'am her saree was beautiful. Yesterday I said her explanation of photosynthesis was "the best in the whole school." Last week I carried her books to the staffroom three times.
The internal marks list goes up on Friday. I'm two marks short of an A.
After class today, I said, "Ma'am, you're my favourite teacher. Is there any way I could get two extra marks for my project?"
She smiled, but it wasn't her normal smile. "Rajni, thank you. But marks are for the work. If you want, I'll show you what was missing and you can redo that part."
My face burned the whole way home.
The worst thing is that I do like her. But I didn't say the saree thing because I liked it. I said it because of Friday. And I think she knew.

qa.q: How many marks short of an A is Rajni?
qa.a: Rajni is two marks short of an A.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on the way home?
qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed and ashamed, her face burning, because Rajni knew the praise had been aimed at marks.

qa.q: What would be a better way for Rajni to improve her mark?
qa.a: Rajni could accept Ma'am's offer to see what was missing and redo that part of the project.

qa.q: How might Ritu Ma'am have seen the compliments?
qa.a: Ritu Ma'am probably noticed they were leading up to a request, which is why her smile changed.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows flattering a teacher to win marks and realising the praise was aimed at an outcome, not at the person.

passage:
In the government school of the village, everyone knew Zeenat Didi, the head girl, would choose who led the Republic Day dance.
So all week, Sangeeta made a point of finding her. On Monday she said Zeenat Didi's handwriting was the prettiest in the school. On Tuesday she brought her guavas from the tree at home. On Wednesday she told the other girls, loudly enough for Didi to hear, that Didi was the kindest senior ever.
On Thursday, Sangeeta asked, "Didi, will you pick me for the front?"
Zeenat looked at her for a moment. "You've been very sweet this week, Sangeeta. But you've never talked to me before Monday."
Sangeeta's ears went hot.
"Dance for me after school," Zeenat said, not unkindly. "If your steps are good, you'll be in front. The guavas don't count."
Sangeeta nodded, feeling small and relieved at the same time.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta bring Zeenat Didi on Tuesday?
qa.a: She brought her guavas from the tree at home.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Zeenat said she had never talked to her before Monday?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed, her ears going hot, because her flattery had clearly been seen as aimed at the dance lead.

qa.q: What fair way did Zeenat offer instead of flattery?
qa.a: Zeenat asked Sangeeta to dance after school, so the choice would depend on her steps, not on the guavas or praise.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see the week of compliments?
qa.a: Zeenat sees them as aimed at getting the front position rather than real friendship, though she responds kindly.

grounding: It shows a teenager flattering an older student to win a dance position, praise aimed at an outcome rather than the person.

passage: In the school library in Melbourne, Tuan rehearsed under his breath before Nour, the Year 12 captain of the debate team, came in. Trials for the last spot were on Friday. "Your speech at assembly was honestly the best thing I've heard all year," he said, sliding into the seat beside her. He hadn't actually listened to most of it. He praised her notes, her shoes, the way she ran meetings. Nour smiled, then asked, "Which part of the speech did you like?" Tuan's mind went blank. "Uh, all of it?" She nodded slowly and went back to her notes. Walking home past the tram stop, Tuan kept replaying that pause. He had wanted her vote, not her speech, and she had probably felt the difference. He decided to turn up on Friday with his best argument instead.

qa.q: When were trials for the last spot on the debate team?
qa.a: Trials for the last spot were on Friday.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when Nour asked which part of the speech he liked?
qa.a: Tuan felt caught and embarrassed, because he hadn't listened to most of the speech and his praise was aimed at winning her vote.

qa.q: What could Tuan try instead of heaping on compliments?
qa.a: He could earn the spot with his own argument at trials, and keep praise for moments when he means something specific.

qa.q: How might Nour see Tuan's compliments after that pause?
qa.a: Nour may sense the praise was empty and aimed at the trial, which could make her trust his later compliments less.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager heaping compliments on an older student to win a team place, with the praise aimed at an outcome rather than at her.
